text:
The debate over whether tipping should be abolished has been ongoing, with some arguing that it is an essential part of the service industry and others believing it to be unfair and exploitative. In this essay, I will argue that tipping should indeed be abolished, comparing two alternative systems before taking a position.

One alternative system to tipping is that employed in many European countries, where a service charge is automatically added to the bill. This approach has been successful in reducing income inequality among servers, as it ensures that all workers receive a fair wage regardless of their tips. However, this system also has its drawbacks, such as limiting customer discretion and potentially leading to overcharging.

Another alternative is the model used in Japan, where tipping is considered impolite and service staff are paid a living wage. This approach prioritizes fairness and respect for workers' dignity over customer generosity. While it may not be feasible to implement a system where customers do not tip at all, it highlights the importance of reevaluating our cultural norms surrounding gratuities.

However, one potential counterargument to abolishing tipping is that it would lead to reduced wages for service staff. For instance, if servers were paid a living wage by their employers, they might rely more heavily on part-time or seasonal work to supplement their income. But I argue that this concern can be mitigated through legislation and employer-employee negotiations.

For example, in the United States, cities like Seattle have implemented laws requiring certain employers to provide a higher minimum wage to tipped workers. This demonstrates that it is possible to balance the need for fair compensation with customer generosity. Moreover, if customers were accustomed to paying service charges instead of tips, servers would be more likely to receive consistent and substantial income from each shift.

One specific case illustrates why tipping should be abolished: the story of Danny Bowien's restaurant, Mission Chinese Food in San Francisco. In 2015, after being tipped for 15 years, the head chef revealed that he had been earning only $14 per hour, despite raking in over $50,000 a year from tips. This example highlights the inherent exploitation in tipping systems, where workers are forced to rely on unpredictable and often meager gratuities to make ends meet.

In conclusion, while alternative systems like service charges or living wages have their merits, I believe that abolishing tipping would be the most equitable solution for the service industry. By phasing out tipping and implementing a higher minimum wage for tipped workers, we can prioritize fairness and respect for all employees' dignity.
